claim: C57BL6/J male mice were fed either a control or high-fat diet for 10 weeks beginning at 6 weeks of age.
source: C57BL6/J male mice were fed either a control or high-fat diet for 10 weeks beginning at 6 weeks of age.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the experimental design.

claim: Males were timed-mated with control-fed C57BL6/J females to generate pregnancies, followed by collection of sperm, and placentas at embryonic day (E)14.5.
source: Males were timed-mated with control-fed C57BL6/J females to generate pregnancies, followed by collection of sperm, and placentas at embryonic day (E)14.5.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for generating pregnancies and collecting samples.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation targeting histone H3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) was performed on sperm to define obesity-associated changes in enrichment.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation targeting histone H3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) was performed on sperm to define obesity-associated changes in enrichment.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to analyze sperm chromatin.

claim: Paternal obesity corresponded with altered sperm H3K4me3 at promoters of genes involved in metabolism and development.
source: Paternal obesity corresponded with altered sperm H3K4me3 at promoters of genes involved in metabolism and development.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Altered sperm H3K4me3 was localized at placental enhancers.
source: Notably, altered sperm H3K4me3 was also localized at placental enhancers.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Bulk RNA-sequencing on placentas revealed paternal obesity-associated sex-specific changes in expression of genes involved in hypoxic processes such as angiogenesis, nutrient transport, and imprinted genes.
source: Bulk RNA-sequencing on placentas revealed paternal obesity-associated sex-specific changes in expression of genes involved in hypoxic processes such as angiogenesis, nutrient transport, and imprinted genes, with a subset of de-regulated genes showing changes in H3K4me3 in sperm at corresponding promoters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNA-seq analysis stated in the abstract.

claim: A subset of de-regulated genes in placentas showed changes in H3K4me3 in sperm at corresponding promoters.
source: Bulk RNA-sequencing on placentas revealed paternal obesity-associated sex-specific changes in expression of genes involved in hypoxic processes such as angiogenesis, nutrient transport, and imprinted genes, with a subset of de-regulated genes showing changes in H3K4me3 in sperm at corresponding promoters.
evidence: This describes a correlation between sperm epigenetic changes and placental gene expression.

claim: Paternal obesity was linked to impaired placenta development, specifically altered trophoblast cell lineage specification.
source: Paternal obesity was also linked to impaired placenta development; specifically, a deconvolution analysis revealed altered trophoblast cell lineage specification.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the deconvolution analysis stated in the abstract.

claim: The placenta is an extraembryonic organ that regulates fetal growth and development, and contributes to long-term adult health.
source: The placenta is an extraembryonic organ that regulates fetal growth and development, and contributes to long-term adult health (Regnault et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Regnault et al., 2002.

claim: In the mouse, the cells that give rise to the placenta, the trophectoderm (TE) cell lineage, first appear in the preimplantation blastocyst at embryonic day 3.5 (E3.5).
source: In the mouse, the cells that give rise to the placenta, the trophectoderm (TE) cell lineage, first appear in the preimplantation blastocyst at embryonic day 3.5 (E3.5).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mouse placental development.

claim: Blastocyst implantation begins at E4.5, triggering a cascade of paracrine, endocrine, and immune-related events that participate in endometrial decidualization.
source: Blastocyst implantation begins at E4.5, triggering a cascade of paracrine, endocrine, and immune-related events that participate in endometrial decidualization.
evidence: This describes the timing and biological processes of implantation.

claim: The first placental fate segregation is between the extraembryonic ectoderm and ectoplacental cone (EPC).
source: The first placental fate segregation is between the extraembryonic ectoderm and ectoplacental cone (EPC).
evidence: This describes the developmental lineage specification in the placenta.

claim: Cells of the EPC in direct contact with the decidua give rise to the cells with invasive and endocrine capacity, including trophoblast giants (TGCs), glycocen trophoblast, and spongiotrophoblast (SPT).
source: Cells of the EPC in direct contact with the decidua give rise to the cells with invasive and endocrine capacity, including trophoblast giants (TGCs), glycocen trophoblast, and spongiotrophoblast (SPT).
evidence: This describes the differentiation of EPC cells into specific trophoblast subtypes.

claim: Cells of the chorion will produce two layers of fused, multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast (SynT-I and SynT-II) and sinusoidal TGCs.
source: Cells of the chorion will produce two layers of fused, multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast (SynT-I and SynT-II) and sinusoidal TGCs.
evidence: This describes the differentiation of chorionic cells.

claim: From E8.5, the embryonic allantois becomes fused with the chorion, permitting invagination of mesoderm-derived angiogenic progenitors that form the basis of the placental vascular bed.
source: From E8.5, the embryonic allantois becomes fused with the chorion, permitting invagination of mesoderm-derived angiogenic progenitors that form the basis of the placental vascular bed (Hemberger et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a key developmental event in placental vascularization, supported by citation.

claim: The placental labyrinth zone is functionally critical for sustaining fetal growth throughout gestation.
source: Together, these cells form a transportive interface, the placental labyrinth zone, which is functionally critical for sustaining fetal growth throughout gestation (Rossant and Cross, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rossant and Cross, 2001.

claim: Interhemal transfer between maternal and fetal circulation begins at E10.5.
source: Interhemal transfer between maternal and fetal circulation begins at E10.5, and by E12.5, all terminally differentiated cell types of the mature placenta are present.
evidence: This describes the timing of functional placental development.

claim: By E12.5, all terminally differentiated cell types of the mature placenta are present.
source: Interhemal transfer between maternal and fetal circulation begins at E10.5, and by E12.5, all terminally differentiated cell types of the mature placenta are present.
evidence: This describes the timing of placental cell differentiation.

claim: Genetic studies of placental development using mouse mutants have identified key genes for development, differentiation, maintenance, and function.
source: Genetic studies of placental development using mouse mutants have identified key genes for development, differentiation, maintenance, and function (Perez-Garcia et al., 2018; Rossant and Cross, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perez-Garcia et al., 2018 and Rossant and Cross, 2001.

claim: Homeobox transcription factors are required for trophoblast lineage development (e.g. genes Cdx2, Eomes).
source: For example, homeobox transcription factors are required for trophoblast lineage development (e.g. genes Cdx2, Eomes) (Chawengsaksophak et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2013; Ciruna and Rossant, 1999; Kunath et al., 2004; Russ et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maintenance of SPT requires the genes Ascl2 and Egfr.
source: and maintenance of SPT requires the genes Ascl2 and Egfr (Guillemot et al., 1995; Guillemot et al., 1994; Sibilia and Wagner, 1995; Tanaka et al., 1997; Threadgill et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There exists 228 imprinted genes identified in humans and 260 in mice.
source: There exists 228 imprinted genes identified in humans and 260 in mice; many are strongly expressed in the placenta (Coan et al., 2005; Morison et al., 2005; Tucci et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many imprinted genes are strongly expressed in the placenta.
source: There exists 228 imprinted genes identified in humans and 260 in mice; many are strongly expressed in the placenta (Coan et al., 2005; Morison et al., 2005; Tucci et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Genomic imprinting refers to monoallelic gene expression that is dependent on whether the gene was inherited maternally or paternally.
source: Genomic imprinting refers to monoallelic gene expression that is dependent on whether the gene was inherited maternally or paternally (Ferguson-Smith et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation.

claim: The expression of imprinted genes is regulated by DNA methylation, acting in concert with chromatin modifications, such as histone H3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) and histone H3 lysine 9 di-methylation (H3K9me2).
source: The expression of imprinted genes is regulated by DNA methylation, acting in concert with chromatin modifications, such as histone H3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3) and histone H3 lysine 9 di-methylation (H3K9me2) (Dindot et al., 2009; McEwen and Ferguson-Smith, 2010; Wen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Disruption of placental imprinting is associated with placentation defects and aberrant fetal growth.
source: Importantly, disruption of placental imprinting is associated with placentation defects and aberrant fetal growth (McMinn et al., 2006; Monk, 2015; Zadora et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Placental defects can result in obstetrical complications such as pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, preterm birth, and fetal growth restriction.
source: Placental defects can result in obstetrical complications such as pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, preterm birth, and fetal growth restriction (Brosens et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is associated with a heightened risk for adult-onset cardiometabolic diseases, coronary heart disease, and stroke.
source: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) in turn is associated with a heightened risk for adult-onset cardiometabolic diseases, coronary heart disease, and stroke, supporting a placental role in long-term health of offspring (Brodszki et al., 2005; Crispi et al., 2010; Cruz-Lemini et al., 2016; Eriksson et al., 2016; Menendez-Castro et al., 2018; Mierzynski et al., 2016; Morsing et al., 2014; Sarvari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Placental insufficiency occurs in 10–15% of pregnancies.
source: For example, placental insufficiency occurs in 10–15% of pregnancies, and underlying causes include advanced maternal age (Ales et al., 1990; Torous and Roberts, 2020; Wu et al., 2019), hypertension (Krielessi et al., 2012), obesity (Delhaes et al., 2018; Lutsiv et al., 2015; MacInnis et al., 2016; Mission et al., 2015; Sohlberg et al., 2012), cigarette smoking (Pintican et al., 2019), drug and alcohol use, and medications (Sebastiani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statistical claim supported by citations.

claim: Underlying causes of placental insufficiency include advanced maternal age, hypertension, obesity, cigarette smoking, drug and alcohol use, and medications.
source: For example, placental insufficiency occurs in 10–15% of pregnancies, and underlying causes include advanced maternal age (Ales et al., 1990; Torous and Roberts, 2020; Wu et al., 2019), hypertension (Krielessi et al., 2012), obesity (Delhaes et al., 2018; Lutsiv et al., 2015; MacInnis et al., 2016; Mission et al., 2015; Sohlberg et al., 2012), cigarette smoking (Pintican et al., 2019), drug and alcohol use, and medications (Sebastiani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Emerging studies indicate that the paternal pre-conception environment including diet and obesity also play a critical role in placental development and offspring health.
source: However, emerging studies indicate that the paternal pre-conception environment including diet and obesity also play a critical role in placental development and offspring health (Binder et al., 2015a; Binder et al., 2012; Jazwiec et al., 2022; Lambrot et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Genetic manipulation studies have determined that the paternal genome has greater potential for extraembryonic and trophoblast development compared to the maternal genome.
source: Notably, genetic manipulation studies have determined that the paternal genome has greater potential for extraembryonic and trophoblast development compared to the maternal genome, and paternally expressed genes dominate placenta gene expression (Barton et al., 1985; Barton et al., 1984; Mcgrath and Solter, 1986; McGrath and Solter, 1984; Surani et al., 1984; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Paternally expressed genes dominate placenta gene expression.
source: Notably, genetic manipulation studies have determined that the paternal genome has greater potential for extraembryonic and trophoblast development compared to the maternal genome, and paternally expressed genes dominate placenta gene expression (Barton et al., 1985; Barton et al., 1984; Mcgrath and Solter, 1986; McGrath and Solter, 1984; Surani et al., 1984; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sperm chromatin profiles highly resemble that of TE and placenta tissue.
source: Additionally, we recently showed that sperm chromatin profiles highly resemble that of TE and placenta tissue, and H3K4me3-enriched regions in sperm are expressed in these tissues, highlighting a molecular connection from the male germline to the developing placenta (Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pepin et al., 2022.

claim: H3K4me3-enriched regions in sperm are expressed in TE and placenta tissues.
source: Additionally, we recently showed that sperm chromatin profiles highly resemble that of TE and placenta tissue, and H3K4me3-enriched regions in sperm are expressed in these tissues, highlighting a molecular connection from the male germline to the developing placenta (Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pepin et al., 2022.

claim: Paternal folate deficiency was associated with an altered sperm epigenome, differential gene expression in the placenta, and abnormal fetal development.
source: In mice, we demonstrated that paternal folate deficiency was associated with an altered sperm epigenome, differential gene expression in the placenta, and abnormal fetal development (Lambrot et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lambrot et al., 2013.

claim: Advanced paternal age and toxicant exposure have been linked to altered placental imprinting and reduced placental weight.
source: In other mouse models, advanced paternal age and toxicant exposure have been linked to altered placental imprinting and reduced placental weight, and paternal obesity was linked to alterations in placental DNA methylation, aberrant allocation of cell lineage to TE (Binder et al., 2012; Binder et al., 2015b; Denomme et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Paternal obesity was linked to alterations in placental DNA methylation and aberrant allocation of cell lineage to TE.
source: In other mouse models, advanced paternal age and toxicant exposure have been linked to altered placental imprinting and reduced placental weight, and paternal obesity was linked to alterations in placental DNA methylation, aberrant allocation of cell lineage to TE (Binder et al., 2012; Binder et al., 2015b; Denomme et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Male partner metabolic syndrome and being overweight have been associated with an increased risk for pre-eclampsia and negative pregnancy outcomes.
source: Male partner metabolic syndrome and being overweight have been associated with an increased risk for pre-eclampsia and negative pregnancy outcomes (Lin et al., 2022; Murugappan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Sperm from obese males had aberrant H3K4me3 enrichment at genes implicated in metabolism and placenta development.
source: As we described in our paternal obesity model (Pepin et al., 2022), sperm from obese males had aberrant H3K4me3 enrichment at genes implicated in metabolism and placenta development, and sired offspring with metabolic disturbances (Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pepin et al., 2022.

claim: Obese males sired offspring with metabolic disturbances.
source: As we described in our paternal obesity model (Pepin et al., 2022), sperm from obese males had aberrant H3K4me3 enrichment at genes implicated in metabolism and placenta development, and sired offspring with metabolic disturbances (Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pepin et al., 2022.

claim: Paternal offspring born to obese fathers have impaired whole body energetics and are glucose intolerant.
source: Here, we used sperm and placenta from a similar paternal obesity model described in Jazwiec et al., 2022, where we demonstrated paternal offspring born to obese fathers have impaired whole body energetics and are glucose intolerant.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jazwiec et al., 2022.

claim: Pregnancies sired by obese males were associated with placenta showing characteristics of hypoxia, accompanied by histo-morphological changes in blood vessel integrity.
source: In addition, we showed that pregnancies sired by obese males were associated with placenta showing characteristics of hypoxia, accompanied by histo-morphological changes in blood vessel integrity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jazwiec et al., 2022.

claim: Histological and immunohistology analyses of placentas collected at E14.5 and E18.5 revealed that paternal obesity resulted in significant changes in transcription factors that regulate blood vessel development, blood vessel integrity, and signaling pathways governed by hypoxia (HIF1A, VEGF, and VEGFR-2).
source: Specifically, histological and immunohistology analyses of placentas collected at E14.5 and E18.5 in Jazwiec et al., 2022, revealed that paternal obesity resulted in significant changes in transcription factors that regulate blood vessel development, blood vessel integrity, and signaling pathways governed by hypoxia (HIF1A, VEGF, and VEGFR-2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jazwiec et al., 2022.

claim: Analysis of sequencing data revealed 35,184 regions enriched for H3K4me3.
source: Analysis of sequencing data revealed 35,184 regions enriched for H3K4me3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Materials and methods) that were highly concordant across samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the ChIP-seq data analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) on counts at sperm H3K4me3-enriched regions revealed separation of samples along principal component 1 (PC1) according to dietary treatment.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) on counts at sperm H3K4me3-enriched regions revealed separation of samples along principal component 1 (PC1) according to dietary treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the PCA analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Of the top 5% differentially enriched H3K4me3 (deH3K4me3) regions, some were common to those previously identified in Pepin et al., 2022 (128 overlapping deH3K4me3 regions, Fisher's exact test p=2.2e-16).
source: Of the top 5% and top 10% differentially enriched H3K4me3 (deH3K4me3) regions, some were common to those previously identified in Pepin et al., 2022 (128 and 423 overlapping deH3K4me3 regions, Fisher's exact test p=2.2e-16 and p=2.2e-16, Figure 2—figure supplement 1Di and ii, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison with a previous study, with reference to a figure.

claim: The majority of obesity-sensitive regions showed an increase in enrichment for H3K4me3 (71.4%, n=1257 versus n=503).
source: Focusing on the top 5% regions most impacted by obesity, the majority of regions showed an increase in enrichment for H3K4me3, consistent with our previous study (71.4%, n=1257 versus n=503, Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Regions losing H3K4me3 showed moderate H3K4me3 enrichment in CON sperm, with predominantly low CpG density.
source: Regions losing H3K4me3 showed moderate H3K4me3 enrichment in CON sperm, with predominantly low CpG density, whereas regions gaining H3K4me3 showed low-to-moderate enrichment, with mainly high CpG density (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a characterization of the genomic features of deH3K4me3 regions with reference to a figure.

claim: Regions gaining H3K4me3 showed low-to-moderate enrichment, with mainly high CpG density.
source: Regions losing H3K4me3 showed moderate H3K4me3 enrichment in CON sperm, with predominantly low CpG density, whereas regions gaining H3K4me3 showed low-to-moderate enrichment, with mainly high CpG density (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a characterization of the genomic features of deH3K4me3 regions with reference to a figure.

claim: Regions losing H3K4me3 were predominantly located >5 kilobase (kb) from the transcription start site (TSS), likely at transposable elements, putative enhancer regions, and intergenic regions.
source: Similarly to our previous findings, regions losing H3K4me3 were predominantly located >5 kilobase (kb) from the transcription start site (TSS), likely at transposable elements, putative enhancer regions, and intergenic regions (Figure 2Di; Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a characterization of the genomic location of deH3K4me3 regions with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Regions gaining H3K4me3 in HFD-sperm were located near the TSS (within 1 kb), likely at promoter regions.
source: Regions gaining H3K4me3 in HFD-sperm were located near the TSS (within 1 kb), likely at promoter regions (Figure 2Dii).
evidence: This is a characterization of the genomic location of deH3K4me3 regions with reference to a figure.

claim: Obesity-associated deH3K4me3 at promoter regions detected in each study showed enrichment at similar gene ontology (GO) processes, such as metabolic processes, cellular stress responses, transcription, and development.
source: Furthermore, obesity-associated deH3K4me3 at promoter regions detected in each study showed enrichment at similar gene ontology (GO) processes, such as metabolic processes, cellular stress responses, transcription, and development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary files 1b-d and 2).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Cbx7 (chromobox protein homolog 7) is a component of the polycomb repressive complex 1, involved in transcriptional regulation of genes including the Hox gene family.
source: Examples of genes showing deH3K4me3 in sperm include Cbx7 (chromobox protein homolog 7, a component of the polycomb repressive complex 1, involved in transcriptional regulation of genes including the Hox gene family)
evidence: This is a description of gene function.

claim: Prdx6 (peroxiredoxin 6) is an antioxidant enzyme involved in cell redox regulation by reducing molecules such as hydrogen peroxide and fatty acid hyperoxides.
source: Prdx6 (peroxiredoxin 6, an antioxidant enzyme involved in cell redox regulation by reducing molecules such as hydrogen peroxide and fatty acid hyperoxides)
evidence: This is a description of gene function.

claim: Slc19a1 (solute carrier family 19 member 1 or folate transporter 1) is a folate organic phosphate antiporter involved in the regulation of intracellular folate concentrations.
source: and Slc19a1 (solute carrier family 19 member 1 or folate transporter 1; a folate organic phosphate antiporter involved in the regulation of intracellular folate concentrations) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a description of gene function with reference to a figure.

claim: Igf2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) is a paternally expressed imprinted gene with an essential role in promoting cellular growth and proliferation in the placenta.
source: We identified deH3K4me3 in HFD-sperm at Igf2 (Figure 2Eii – insulin-like growth factor 2), a paternally expressed imprinted gene with an essential role in promoting cellular growth and proliferation in the placenta.
evidence: This is a description of gene function with reference to a figure.

claim: Igf2 was previously shown to be differentially expressed in placentas derived from obese males.
source: Interestingly, Igf2 was also previously shown to be differentially expressed in placentas derived from obese males (Jazwiec et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jazwiec et al., 2022.

claim: The function of the gene Igf2 encoding protein IGF-2 has been related to metabolic disease and obesity.
source: Importantly, the function of the gene Igf2 encoding protein IGF-2 has been related to metabolic disease and obesity (Kadakia and Josefson, 2016; Livingstone and Borai, 2014; reviewed in St-Pierre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Otx2 is a homeodomain-containing TF involved in brain and sense organs development.
source: Other imprinted genes with deH3K4me3 included the homeodomain-containing TF Otx2 (involved in brain and sense organs development)
evidence: This is a description of gene function.

claim: Kcnq1 is a voltage-gated potassium channel gene required for cardiac action potential.
source: and the voltage-gated potassium channel Kcnq1 gene (required for cardiac action potential).
evidence: This is a description of gene function.

claim: Differential H3K4me3 enrichment in HFD-sperm occurred at enhancers involved in placenta development.
source: Notably, deH3K4me3 localized to putative enhancers including at those implicated in gene regulation of the testes, placenta, and embryonic stem cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis with reference to figures and citation.

claim: Three genes potentially regulated by placenta-specific enhancers were paternally expressed imprinted genes (TMEM174, PLAGL1, and PDGFB).
source: Interestingly, when searching for closest genes potentially regulated by placenta-specific enhancers, three were paternally expressed imprinted genes (Tucci et al., 2019). These genes included those coding for the transmembrane protein TMEM174, the zinc finger protein PLAGL1 (a suppressor of cell growth), and the growth factor PDGFB (a member of the protein family of platelet-derived and vascular endothelial growth factors).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis with citation.

claim: PLAGL1 is a zinc finger protein that is a suppressor of cell growth.
source: the zinc finger protein PLAGL1 (a suppressor of cell growth)
evidence: This is a description of gene function.

claim: PDGFB is a growth factor essential for embryonic development, angiogenesis, and cell proliferation and migration.
source: and the growth factor PDGFB (a member of the protein family of platelet-derived and vascular endothelial growth factors). This growth factor is essential for embryonic development, angiogenesis, and cell proliferation and migration.
evidence: This is a description of gene function.

claim: Many TSS in sperm marked by H3K4me3 are enriched for transcription factor (TF) binding sites and bound by components of the transcriptional machinery complex (phosphorylated RNA pol II and Med12).
source: Many TSS in sperm marked by H3K4me3 are enriched for transcription factor (TF) binding sites and bound by components of the transcriptional machinery complex (phosphorylated RNA pol II and Med12).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sperm chromatin.

claim: TF interactions in sperm have been reported to occur at open chromatin regions and suggested to potentially confer gene expression in the embryo.
source: In sperm, such TF interactions have been reported to occur at open chromatin regions and suggested to potentially confer gene expression in the embryo (Jung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jung et al., 2017.

claim: The regions that gained H3K4me3 were significantly enriched for 202 TF binding motifs (p<0.05, binomial statistical test, q-value<0.05).
source: The regions that gained H3K4me3 were significantly enriched for 202 TF binding motifs (p<0.05, binomial statistical test, q-value<0.05; Figure 3 and Supplementary file 3; Heinz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis with reference to figure and supplementary file.

claim: Regions that had reduced H3K4me3 were not significantly enriched for TF binding motifs (q-value>0.05).
source: In contrast, regions that had reduced H3K4me3 were not significantly enriched for TF binding motifs (q-value>0.05).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis.

claim: Of the top 10 motifs enriched at regions with increased H3K4me3 signal in HFD-sperm, these genomic sequences were predicted to be bound by TFs belonging to the ETS, THAP, and ZF motif families (p<1e-10, q-value<0.0001).
source: Of the top 10 motifs enriched at regions with increased H3K4me3 signal in HFD-sperm, these genomic sequences were predicted to be bound by TFs belonging to the ETS, THAP, and ZF motif families (p<1e-10, q-value<0.0001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: SP1, a TF associated with recurrent miscarriage, was found to be among the top TF-associated motif hits (p = 1e-16, q-value<0.0001) in regions gaining H3K4me3 in sperm from obese sires.
source: Of interest, SP1, a TF associated with recurrent miscarriage, was found to be among the top TF-associated motif hits (p = 1e-16, q-value<0.0001) in regions gaining H3K4me3 in sperm from obese sires (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis with citation.

claim: Activating transcription factor 7 (ATF7; p-value=1e-3, q-value=0.0044) binding sites were enriched and this TF has been associated with oxidative stress-induced epigenetic changes in male germ cells in a mouse model of low-protein diet.
source: Activating transcription factor 7 (ATF7; p-value=1e-3, q-value=0.0044, Supplementary file 3) binding sites were also enriched and this TF has been associated with oxidative stress-induced epigenetic changes in male germ cells in a mouse model of low-protein diet (Yoshida et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis with citation.

claim: There were differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in female (n=2035) and male (n=2365) placentas associated with paternal obesity.
source: There were differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in female (n=2035) and male (n=2365) placentas associated with paternal obesity (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Significantly enriched pathways in placentas included genes involved in the transport of cholesterol, angiogenesis, and neurogenesis.
source: Disruption in these functions is suggested in the significantly enriched pathways that included genes involved in the transport of cholesterol, angiogenesis, and neurogenesis (Figure 4C and D, Supplementary file 1e and f).
evidence: This is a result from the GO analysis with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Other significantly enriched processes included genes implicated in nutrient and vitamin transport.
source: Other significantly enriched processes included genes implicated in nutrient and vitamin transport (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is a result from the GO analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The gene Irs1 was found to be differentially expressed in placentas in association with paternal obesity, validating previous findings.
source: Of note, the gene Irs1 was found to be differentially expressed in placentas in association with paternal obesity, validating our previous findings in the initial characterization of the model (Jazwiec et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis with citation.

claim: In HFD-sired female and male placentas, 23 and 28 imprinted genes were differentially expressed, respectively.
source: Given that correct imprinted gene expression is critical for placental growth and development, and that aberrant expression of a single imprinted gene is sufficient to induce placental defects, it is worth noting that in HFD-sired female and male placentas, 23 and 28 imprinted genes were differentially expressed, respectively (Figure 4E and F; Tucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis with reference to figures and citation.

claim: A significant number of DEGs overlapped between female and male placentas (n=359, Fisher's exact test p=1.5e-19).
source: Although a significant number of DEGs overlapped between female and male placentas (n=359, Fisher's exact test p=1.5e-19; Figure 4—figure supplement 1Di)
evidence: This is a statistical result with reference to a figure.

claim: 82% of female DEGs and 85% of male DEGs were uniquely de-regulated in response to paternal obesity.
source: 82% of female DEGs and 85% of male DEGs were uniquely de-regulated in response to paternal obesity.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Paternal obesity was associated with a significant decrease in invasive SPT cell relative abundance in female placentas (p=0.02).

claim: Paternal obesity was associated with an increase in high-Hsd11b2 SPT cells in both male and female placentas (p=0.01 and p=0.06, respectively).

evidence: This is a result from the deconvolution analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: After adjustment for placental cellular composition, 423 DEGs were detected in female placentas and 1487 DEGs in male placentas.

claim: Differential expression of Igf2 was detected in placentas sired by obese sires.
source: Similarly to our previous characterization of the model, here we detected differential expression of Igf2 in placentas sired by obese sires (Jazwiec et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis with citation.

claim: The reduction in the number of detected DEGs before versus after accounting for cellular composition suggests that changes in cell-type proportions at least partly drive tissue-level differential expression.
source: The reduction in the number of detected DEGs before versus after accounting for cellular composition suggests that changes in cell-type proportions at least partly drive tissue-level differential expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Pre-eclampsia-associated cellular heterogeneity in human placentas mediates previously detected bulk gene expression differences.
source: This is consistent with the recent finding that pre-eclampsia-associated cellular heterogeneity in human placentas mediates previously detected bulk gene expression differences (Campbell et al., 2023).

claim: Hypoxia is a tightly regulated process that is essential for proper vascular formation supporting fetal growth during placental development.
source: During placental development, hypoxia is a tightly regulated process that is essential for proper vascular formation supporting fetal growth.
evidence: This is established knowledge about placental development.

claim: Hypoxia is a hallmark of placental insufficiency, reflecting poor oxygen and nutrient supply to the fetus, resulting in fetal growth restriction, low birth weight, and consequently heightened risk for cardiometabolic disease.
source: Hypoxia is also a hallmark of placental insufficiency, reflecting poor oxygen and nutrient supply to the fetus, resulting in fetal growth restriction, low birth weight, and consequently heightened risk for cardiometabolic disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about placental pathology.

claim: Placentas derived from obese sires, like hypoxic placentas, exhibit changes in gene expression and altered angiogenesis, vasculature, and development.
source: Placentas derived from obese sires, like hypoxic placentas, exhibit changes in gene expression and altered angiogenesis, vasculature, and development (Binder et al., 2015a; Binder et al., 2012; Jazwiec et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2022; McPherson et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 2017, this study).

claim: In the IUGR mouse model, hypoxia was induced during late gestation, which resulted in pregnancies with aberrant placental transcriptome, IUGR, decreased birth weights, and offspring exhibiting adult-onset cardiometabolic disturbances.
source: In this model, hypoxia was induced during late gestation, which resulted in pregnancies with aberrant placental transcriptome, IUGR, decreased birth weights, and offspring exhibiting adult-onset cardiometabolic disturbances (Chu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chu et al., 2019.

claim: Differential analysis of the IUGR mouse model identified 1935 DEGs in hypoxic placentas.
source: This differential analysis identified 1935 DEGs in hypoxic placentas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a result from the differential expression analysis with reference to figures.

claim: A total of 17 different cell types were detected in the deconvolution analysis of hypoxic placentas.
source: Likewise, we applied our deconvolution analysis described above to this bulk RNA-seq data from hypoxic placentas and detected the same principal cell types as those detected in our samples; a total of 17 different cell types were detected (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the deconvolution analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The proportion values for each individual cell types were highly comparable across placentas from the HFD-sire and the hypoxia mouse models.
source: Remarkably, the proportion values for each individual cell types were highly comparable across placentas from the HFD-sire and the hypoxia mouse models (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Hypoxic placentas showed a significant decrease in invasive SPT cell abundance (p=0.003).
source: Similarly to placentas derived from obese sires, hypoxic placentas showed a significant decrease in invasive SPT cell abundance (p=0.003, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from the deconvolution analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Hypoxic placentas showed a significant increase in progenitor trophoblast (Gjb3-high), primitive endoderm (PE) lineage (Gkn2-high), erythroblast (Hbb-y-high), and endodermal (Afp-high) cells, compared to control (p=0.000004, p=0.01, p=0.000003, p=0.005, respectively).
source: Hypoxic placentas also showed a significant increase in progenitor trophoblast (Gjb3-high), primitive endoderm (PE) lineage (Gkn2-high), erythroblast (Hbb-y-high), and endodermal (Afp-high) cells, compared to control (p=0.000004, p=0.01, p=0.000003, p=0.005, respectively; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from the deconvolution analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Accounting for cell-type proportions allowed for the detection of 1477 DEGs associated with hypoxia and growth restriction.
source: Accounting for cell-type proportions allowed for the detection of 1477 DEGs associated with hypoxia and growth restriction (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is a result from the adjusted differential expression analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: 356 DEGs overlapped with those initially detected before cellular composition adjustment (24%, Fisher's exact test p=8.4e-15).
source: of which 356 overlapped with those initially detected before cellular composition adjustment (24%, Fisher's exact test p=8.4e-15; Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a statistical result with reference to a figure.

claim: After adjusting for cell-type proportions, 207 of the paternal-obesity-induced dysregulated genes in male placentas were also found to be differentially expressed in hypoxic placentas (Fisher's exact test p=5.1e-16).
source: Importantly, after adjusting for cell-type proportions, 207 of the paternal-obesity-induced dysregulated genes in male placentas were also found to be differentially expressed in hypoxic placentas (Fisher's exact test p=5.1e-16; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a statistical result with reference to a figure.

claim: A key gene supporting the similarity in the molecular pathology of hypoxic placenta and obese sired placenta was the dysregulation of the imprinted gene Igf2.
source: A key gene supporting this similarity in the molecular pathology of hypoxic placenta and obese sired placenta was the dysregulation of the imprinted gene Igf2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Both models resulted in metabolic disturbances in offspring, supporting the role of the placenta at the origin of paternally induced metabolic maladaptation.
source: Furthermore, both models resulted in metabolic disturbances in offspring, supporting the role of the placenta at the origin of paternally induced metabolic maladaptation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Paternal obesity, like gestational hypoxia, induces pathological and molecular characteristics that are hallmarks of placental insufficiency.
source: Collectively, our comparative analyses of placental transcriptomic data from both models indicate that paternal obesity, like gestational hypoxia, induces pathological and molecular characteristics that are hallmarks of placental insufficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis.

claim: Paternal health and environmental exposures impact the establishment of the sperm epigenome and are associated with altered development of the placenta, embryo, and offspring health.
source: Paternal health and environmental exposures impact the establishment of the sperm epigenome and are associated with altered development of the placenta, embryo, and offspring health.
evidence: This is a general statement summarizing existing knowledge.

claim: Paternal obesity is associated with altered sperm chromatin, specifically H3K4me3, and changes in the placental transcriptome.
source: Our findings build on prior knowledge to show that paternal obesity is associated with altered sperm chromatin, specifically H3K4me3, and changes in the placental transcriptome.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Paternal obesity influences the placenta transcriptome and this is one mechanism that could underlie paternally induced placental pathogenesis, growth impeded embryo development, and adult-onset metabolic phenotypes.
source: We show that paternal obesity influences the placenta transcriptome and this is one mechanism that could underlie paternally induced placental pathogenesis, growth impeded embryo development, and adult-onset metabolic phenotypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Paternal HFD-induced obesity alters the placental transcriptome in a sex-specific manner.
source: We further observed that paternal HFD-induced obesity alters the placental transcriptome in a sex-specific manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: There is strong evidence demonstrating sex disparity in metabolic phenotypes and cardiometabolic disease risks.
source: There is strong evidence demonstrating sex disparity in metabolic phenotypes and cardiometabolic disease risks (reviewed in Tramunt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Sex-specific effects are thought to be driven by sex chromosomes, hormonal factors, the gut microbiome, as well as differential fetal programming across sex in response to pre-conception and in utero exposures.
source: These sex-specific effects are thought to be driven by sex chromosomes, hormonal factors, the gut microbiome, as well as differential fetal programming across sex in response to pre-conception and in utero exposures (reviewed in Sandovici et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Some of the postnatal metabolic disturbances observed in paternally induced offspring sexually dimorphic phenotypes are established in the placenta.
source: Here, our findings suggest some of the postnatal metabolic disturbances observed in paternally induced offspring sexually dimorphic phenotypes are established in the placenta.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The placenta is a key organ for imprinted gene function.
source: These genes are epigenetically controlled and inherited in a parent-of-origin manner, and the placenta is a key organ for imprinted gene function (Wood and Oakey, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: According to the conflict hypothesis, maternally imprinted genes (paternally expressed) support fetal growth, whereas paternally imprinted genes (maternally expressed) restrict fetal growth.
source: According to the conflict hypothesis, maternally imprinted genes (paternally expressed) support fetal growth, whereas paternally imprinted genes (maternally expressed) restrict fetal growth (Bressan et al., 2009; Haig and Graham, 1991; Moore and Haig, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deletion of the gene Htra3 in mice has been implicated in IUGR owing to the disorganization of placental labyrinthine capillaries and thereby affecting offspring growth trajectories postnatally.
source: For example, deletion of the gene Htra3 (identified here as a DEG in female placentas) in mice has been implicated in IUGR owing to the disorganization of placental labyrinthine capillaries and thereby affecting offspring growth trajectories postnatally (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The maternally expressed gene Copg2 has been associated with pregnancies with small for gestational age infants.
source: The maternally expressed gene Copg2 (identified here as a DEG in female placentas) has been associated with pregnancies with small for gestational age infants (Kappil et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Loss of the paternally expressed gene Snx14 in mice causes severe placental pathology involving aberrant SynT differentiation, leading to mid-gestation embryonic lethality.
source: Loss of the paternally expressed gene Snx14 in mice (identified here as a DEG in female placentas) causes severe placental pathology involving aberrant SynT differentiation, leading to mid-gestation embryonic lethality (Bryant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The paternally expressed gene Zdbf2 has been implicated in reduced fetal growth in mice, associated with altered appetite signals in the hypothalamic circuit.
source: The paternally expressed gene Zdbf2 (DEG in male placentas) has been implicated in reduced fetal growth in mice, associated with altered appetite signals in the hypothalamic circuit (Glaser et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Placental deficiency of the paternally expressed gene Slc38a2 leads to fetal growth restriction in mice.
source: Placental deficiency of the paternally expressed gene Slc38a2 (identified here as a DEG in male placentas) leads to fetal growth restriction in mice (Vaughan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Mice deficient for the paternally expressed transcriptional co-repressor Tle3 show abnormal placental development including TGC differentiation failure, resulting in fetal death.
source: Lastly, mice deficient for the paternally expressed transcriptional co-repressor Tle3 (identified here as a DEG in male placentas) show abnormal placental development including TGC differentiation failure, resulting in fetal death (Gasperowicz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Disrupting the expression of a single imprinted gene can result in placental defect and consequently compromise fetal health or survival.
source: Importantly, disrupting the expression of a single imprinted gene can result in placental defect and consequently compromise fetal health or survival.
evidence: This is established knowledge about imprinted genes.

claim: The differential expression of imprinted genes detected in female and male placentas as a result of paternal obesity could at least partly explain metabolic phenotypes observed in this mouse model.
source: It is therefore likely that the differential expression of imprinted genes detected in female and male placentas as a result of paternal obesity could at least partly explain metabolic phenotypes observed in this mouse model (Jazwiec et al., 2022; Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations.

claim: Changes in sperm DNA methylation upon HFD feeding has been previously reported.
source: Interestingly, changes in sperm DNA methylation upon HFD feeding has been previously reported, and ETS motifs (enriched in obesity-associated deH3K4me3 in sperm) have been found to be DNA methylation sensitive, including in spermatogonial stem cells (Domcke et al., 2015; Dura et al., 2022; Lea et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ETS motifs have been found to be DNA methylation sensitive, including in spermatogonial stem cells.
source: Interestingly, changes in sperm DNA methylation upon HFD feeding has been previously reported, and ETS motifs (enriched in obesity-associated deH3K4me3 in sperm) have been found to be DNA methylation sensitive, including in spermatogonial stem cells (Domcke et al., 2015; Dura et al., 2022; Lea et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: HFD-induced epimutations at H3K4me3 or DNA methylation could influence one another.
source: Given the interplay between H3K4 and DNA methylation, it is conceivable that HFD-induced epimutations at either of these marks could influence one another (reviewed in Janssen and Lorincz, 2022), and these could in turn alter TF functions.
evidence: This is speculation based on known interplay, supported by citation to a review.

claim: In a mouse model of paternal low-protein diet, oxidative stress-induced phosphorylation of the ATF7 TF was suggested to impede its DNA-binding affinity in germ cells, leading to a decrease in H3K9me2 at target regions.
source: This phenomenon has been described in a mouse model of paternal low-protein diet, where oxidative stress-induced phosphorylation of the ATF7 TF was suggested to impede its DNA-binding affinity in germ cells, leading to a decrease in H3K9me2 at target regions (Yoshida et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

source: As in the low-protein diet model, oxidative stress is a hallmark of obesity and increased levels of reactive oxygen species have been observed in testes of diet-induced obesity mouse models and linked to impaired embryonic development (Fullston et al., 2012; Lane et al., 2014; Mitchell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

source: In addition, the limited overlap between sperm deH3K4me3 and placenta DEGs may also reflect the terminally differentiated state and heterogenous nature of the placenta at E14.5.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the results.

source: Perhaps a greater correspondence between sperm deH3K4me3 may have been observed at earlier developmental time points such as at first lineage segregation corresponding to trophoblast formation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future findings.

source: Indeed, we previously showed by in silico analysis that most regions bearing H3K4me3 in sperm are enriched for this mark in TE, correlate with TE H3K4me3 signal, and correspond to genes expressed in TE (Pepin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pepin et al., 2022.

source: Interestingly, many GO terms related to inflammatory processes were enriched in the obesity-induced deH3K4me3 in sperm (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 1c, and Pepin et al., 2022), suggesting sperm deH3K4me3 might be partly influencing placental inflammation.
evidence: This is a result from the GO analysis with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Sperm deH3K4me3 might be partly influencing placental inflammation.
source: Interestingly, many GO terms related to inflammatory processes were enriched in the obesity-induced deH3K4me3 in sperm (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 1c, and Pepin et al., 2022), suggesting sperm deH3K4me3 might be partly influencing placental inflammation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the GO analysis results.

claim: Many of the DEGs in the paternal obese-sired placentas were involved in the regulation of the heart and brain.
source: Many of the DEGs in the paternal obese-sired placentas were involved in the regulation of the heart and brain.
evidence: This is a result from the GO analysis.

claim: Paternal obesity is associated with the developmental origins of neurological, cardiovascular, and metabolic disease in offspring.
source: This is in line with paternal obesity associated with the developmental origins of neurological, cardiovascular, and metabolic disease in offspring (Andescavage and Limperopoulos, 2021; Binder et al., 2015a; Binder et al., 2012; Chambers et al., 2016; Cropley et al., 2016; de Castro Barbosa et al., 2016; Fullston et al., 2012; Fullston et al., 2013; Grandjean et al., 2015; Huypens et al., 2016; Jazwiec et al., 2022; Mitchell et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2010; Pepin et al., 2022; Perez-Garcia et al., 2018; Terashima et al., 2015; Thornburg et al., 2016; Thornburg and Marshall, 2015; Ueda et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2014).

source: The brain-placenta and heart-placenta axes refer to their developmental linkage to the trophoblast which produces various hormones, neurotransmitters, and growth factors that are central to brain and heart development (Parrettini et al., 2020; Rosenfeld, 2021).

source: This is further illustrated in studies where placental pathology is linked to cardiovascular and heart abnormalities (Andescavage and Limperopoulos, 2021; Thornburg et al., 2016; Thornburg and Marshall, 2015).

source: Notably, neural crest cells are of ectodermal origin which arises from the TE (Prasad et al., 2019), which is in turn governed by paternally driven gene expression.

source: During placentation, invasive SPT have the ability to migrate and invade the maternal-fetal interface and replace maternal vascular endothelial cells, a critical step for maternal arterial remodeling to facilitate low resistance and high volume blood flow to the fetus (Silva and Serakides, 2016).

source: In the placenta, HSD11B2 is responsible for the conversion of cortisol into its inactive form, cortisone, which limits fetal exposure to maternal glucocorticoid levels.

claim: Six-week-old C57BL/6J male mice were co-housed (2 per cage) and randomly allocated to either the control (n=8; CON; standard chow diet, Harlan 8640, Teklad 22/5 Rodent Diet; 17% kcal fat, 54% kcal carbohydrates, 29% kcal protein, 3 kcal/g) or HFD (n=16; HFD; Research Diets Inc, D12492; 20% kcal protein, 20% kcal carbohydrates, 60% kcal fat, 5.21 kcal/g) group, for 10–12 weeks.
source: Six-week-old C57BL/6J male mice were co-housed (2 per cage) and randomly allocated to either the control (n=8; CON; standard chow diet, Harlan 8640, Teklad 22/5 Rodent Diet; 17% kcal fat, 54% kcal carbohydrates, 29% kcal protein, 3 kcal/g) or HFD (n=16; HFD; Research Diets Inc, D12492; 20% kcal protein, 20% kcal carbohydrates, 60% kcal fat, 5.21 kcal/g) group, for 10–12 weeks.

claim: Male mice fed a HFD became significantly heavier weighing approximately 40 g (20 g in weight gain); had elevated body adiposity; elevated fasting blood glucose; were glucose intolerant; had significantly increased serum insulin concentrations, and were insulin resistant as assessed by HOMA-IR.
source: As reported in our previous work, male mice fed a HFD became significantly heavier weighing approximately 40 g (20 g in weight gain); had elevated body adiposity; elevated fasting blood glucose; were glucose intolerant; had significantly increased serum insulin concentrations, and were insulin resistant as assessed by HOMA-IR (Jazwiec et al., 2022).

claim: High-fat male mice had impaired mating efficiency.
